newsitem.title: USA: Dole sees Powell as"a star" in his administration.
newsitem.headline: Dole sees Powell as"a star" in his administration.

text.p: Republican candidate Bob Dole said Wednesday Gulf War hero Colin Powell would be "a star" in his administration should he defeat President Clinton in next month's election.

In his strongest statement yet that the former chairman of the military Joint Chiefs if Staff would be tapped for a major job, Dole told reporters in suburban Chicago: "Colin Powell is going to be one of the stars in our new administration."

He did not say what role Powell -- a retired four-star general whom many Americans have told pollsters they prefer over Dole or Clinton -- might play, but speculation has focused on secretary of state or defence.
Earlier this week, Dole said he had been discussing positions in his administration with several senior party figures, including Powell.

Powell, 59, who decided against launching his own bid for the White House and later spurned overtures from Dole to run as his vice presidential candidate, has said he would consider accepting a cabinet appointment.

Dole plunged into the battleground Midwest on Wednesday, fielding questions from women small business owners at a forum where he stuck to familiar campaign themes of tax cuts and fighting illegal drugs.
When one supporter there demanded to know when Dole would put on "boxing gloves" against the Democratic president she called "slick," Dole didn't take the bait.
"There's a very fine line because there's a myth out there that Bob Dole is mean," Dole replied calmly. "I never thought I was mean."
"He may have a few surprises come next Wednesday," he said, referring to his second scheduled debate with Clinton.
In the first debate last weekend, Dole also shunned a chance to launch into a broadside against Clinton's character.

At the Acme Screw Co. in Chicago, Dole fielded questions from a pre-selected group of businesswomen, an apparent attempt to close the gender gap that is a major factor in Clinton's lead in the opinion polls.
The most aggressive he got was to say "I'm not Bill Clinton, I'm Bob Dole -- I'll give you my word," regarding voter scepticism about his pledge to cut taxes.
On Tuesday Dole stressed his trustworthiness versus what he said was Clinton's record of broken and empty promises. He even referred once to the president as "Bozo."
Speaking about that remark on Wednesday, Dole told reporters, "I didn't make it. You guys didn't listen well enough."

What happened -- and the moment was tape-recorded -- was a supporter near a line where Dole was shaking hands called out, "Please get Bozo out of the White House," and Dole replied, "Bozo's on his way out."

That interchange as well as other attacks on Clinton's trustworthiness led to headlines about "going negative," but spokesman Nelson Warfield told reporters aboard Dole's campaign jet that the campaign had not made any strategic decisions to attack Clinton's character.
"He (Dole) had an opportunity in the first debate to delve into President Clinton's personal life, and he chose not to," Warfield said. "I think he'll be consistent about that."

Forced to cancel half of his campaign appearances in New Jersey on Tuesday because of bad weather, Dole had a light campaign schedule on Wednesday considering that the election is a month away and he is behind in the polls.

He participated in one radio talk show interview and worked in his Washington office on Wednesday morning, then flew to Chicago, where he scheduled two events late in the day before watching the vice presidential debate at a private home in a Chicago suburb on Wednesday night.
"I think Jack Kemp clearly won the debate," he said afterwards of his running mate's performance.
